en: Parivāra 10.
Gāthāsaṅgaṇika 1.
The Training Rule Enacted Concerning the Seven Cities.
“Having arranged his robe over one shoulder and raising his joined palms,
he appeared as if full of longing.”
“From where have you come here?
“In the two Vinayas that have been laid down,
those [rules] which appear in the recitations during the Uposatha ceremonies;”
“How many training rules do you have,
and in how many cities were they laid down?
“Your insight is excellent.”
You inquire with systematic thoroughness;
truly, I shall explain it to you,
just as you are skillful in this matter.
“Those rules laid down in the two Vinayas that come up for recitation at the Uposatha days number three hundred and fifty.”
“They were laid down in seven cities.
“In which seven cities were they laid down?
Pray, explain this to me.”
Having listened to those words,
let us act so that it may lead to our welfare.
[In Vesālī and Rājagaha...]
"At Sāvatthī and Āḷavī;
at Kosambī and among the Sakyas,
as well as among the Bhaggas, they were thus prescribed."
“How many were prescribed at Vesālī?
How many were made at Rājagaha?
How many are there at Sāvatthī?”
"How many were made at Āḷavī?
How many were laid down at Kosambī?
How many are spoken of among the Sakyans?"
“How many blessings were proclaimed by the Blessed One?
Tell me that when asked.
“Ten blessings were proclaimed at Vesālī.”
Twenty-one were performed in Rājagaha;
two hundred and ninety-four were all performed in Sāvatthī.
Six were prescribed at Āḷavī,
eight were enacted at Kosambī;
eight are spoken of among the Sakyans.
Three were prescribed among the Bhaggas;
those that were prescribed at Vesālī,
hear them as they truly are.
Sexual intercourse, the formal act, and further;
extra black [wool];
prepared food, and food passed on from one to another.
The tooth-stick, the naked ascetic,
and the abuse of the bhikkhunīs—
these ten were enacted at Vesālī.
Those things prescribed at Rājagaha—
listen to them as they truly are:
regarding the taking of what is not given at Rājagaha...
Two on disparaging, and two on causing schism;
the inner robe, money, thread,
censuring, and food obtained by prompting.
Eating in a group, at the wrong time,
wandering for alms, bathing, fewer than twenty [monks],
and giving a robe while directing [the donor].
These were performed at Rājagaha;
likewise, twenty-one [were performed] at Giraggacariyā through the giving of one’s will.
Those which were laid down at Sāvatthī,
listen to them as they truly are:
the four pārājika offenses.
There are sixteen Saṅghādisesas,
two Aniyatas,
and twenty-four Nissaggiyas;
One hundred and forty-five are said to be the minor [suttas],
and ten are indeed those to be honored.
And seventy-two rules of training;
two hundred ninety-four in total—
all were enacted at Sāvatthī.
Listen to how those things prescribed at Āḷavī truly are:
the hut, the silk bedding, and—
"Go, O deity, to Khaṇana;
they are sprinkling water containing living beings.
These six were done at Āḷavī."
Listen as they truly were laid down at Kosambī:
the Great Monastery and difficult-to-correctness.
Another door for liquor,
disrespect as a concurrent dharma,
and drinking milk— this is the eighth.
Listen to those things prescribed among the Sakyans exactly as they are:
woolen cloth and the alms-bowl.
Exhortation and medicine,
the needle, and the forest-dweller—
these eight are from Kāpilavatthu.
The instruction on purification by water is proclaimed among the bhikkhunīs;
those which were laid down for the Bhaggas—
Listen to this as it truly is:
having composed themselves,
they fan [the fire] with meat together with rice.
There are four offenses involving defeat,
there are offenses requiring a formal meeting of the Sangha,
and seven offenses involving forfeiture.
Eight and thirty-two minor rules;
two blameworthy, three for those in training—
these are the fifty-six training precepts.
Laid down by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun, in six cities:
three hundred less six.
All were composed at Sāvatthī by the compassionate Buddha,
the illustrious Gotama.
2. The Four Failings:
“That which we asked you, you have explained to us;
each answer has been given without deviation.”
I ask you another thing; please tell me that:
what is heavy and what is light, what has a remainder and what is without remainder, what is grave and what is not grave.
And those [offenses] up to the third [admonition];
the common and the uncommon;
and the classifications by which they are settled through the means of pacification.
“Explain all of these to us;
indeed, let us hear your words.
“There are thirty-one [fetters] that are heavy...”
In this context, all [offenses] are included without exception:
those that are grave are serious (duṭṭhulla),
and those that are serious constitute a failure in virtue (sīlavipatti).
A pārājika and a saṅghādisesa are called "failure in virtue" (sīlavipatti).
A thullaccaya and a pācittiya—
An offense of confession (pāṭidesanīya), an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),
and that which is ill-spoken (dubbhāsita)— and he who,
with the intention of joking, reviles [another].
This is what is considered a failure in conduct:
they hold perverted views,
being led astray by unwholesome qualities.
Those of poor wisdom, shrouded in delusion, misrepresent the Fully Awakened One;
this is what is considered a failure of view.
For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one who has evil desires and is overcome by desire falsely claims non-existent, unreal superhuman states;
for the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one engages in matchmaking;

for the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one says, “The monk who dwells in your monastery is an arahant”; for the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, a monk [accepts] exquisite foods...
She eats having requested [food] for her own sake; for the sake of livelihood, for the cause of livelihood, a bhikkhunī eats fine foods having requested them for her own sake;
for the sake of livelihood, for the cause of livelihood, not being ill, she eats either soup or rice having requested it for her own sake.
This is what is recognized as failure in livelihood.
Listen now to those [offenses] that require a formal act up to the third time, exactly as they are.
The one who follows after the suspended,
the eight cases of "up to the third time," Ariṭṭha, and Caṇḍakāḷī.
“These are your [offenses] up to the third time.
3. On Cutting Off, etc.:
“How many are the offenses involving cutting off?”
How many are offenses involving breaking?
How many are offenses involving tearing? How many are *pācittiya* offenses for which there is no other [expiation]?
How many formal permissions for monks (bhikkhusammuti)?
How many modes of proper conduct (sāmīci)?
How many limits (paramāni)?
“How many are declared by the Buddha,
the Kinsman of the Sun,
as things to be cut off? “Six things to be cut off.”
One offense involving breaking;
one offense involving peeling;
four offenses of expiation for eating what is not left over.
Four formal acts of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
seven forms of courtesy;
fourteen supreme things.
"These sixteen are known and proclaimed by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.
4. Asādhāraṇa, etc.
“Two hundred and twenty training rules for bhikkhus come up for recitation on the Uposatha days.”
Three hundred and four training rules for bhikkhunīs come up for recitation during the Uposatha days.
Forty rules for bhikkhus that are not shared with bhikkhunīs,
and one hundred and thirty for bhikkhunīs.
Not shared with the bhikkhus.
One hundred and seventy-six are not shared by both.
One hundred and seventy-four for both, being equal in training;
two hundred and ten.
The training rules for the bhikkhus come up for recitation during the Uposatha days;
listen to them as they truly are.
There are four offenses involving defeat (pārājika),
thirteen offenses requiring formal meeting of the Sangha (saṅghādisesa),
and two undetermined offenses (aniyata).
There are exactly thirty rules involving forfeiture,
ninety-two minor rules,
and four rules to be confessed.
There are seventy-five rules of training (sekhiya);
these two hundred and twenty are the training precepts (sikkhāpada) for bhikkhus.
They come to the recitation at the Uposatha days.
There are three hundred and forty training rules for bhikkhunīs.
They come for recitation at the Uposatha days;
hear them from me exactly as they are:
the eight offenses involving defeat (pārājika).
There are seventeen Saṅghādisesa rules;
thirty Nissaggiya rules;
and one hundred and sixty-six [Pācittiya rules].
The Minor Rules are thus declared:
the eight offenses requiring confession and the seventy-five rules of training.
There are these three hundred and four training rules for bhikkhunīs;
they come up for recitation on the Uposatha days.
There are forty-four offenses for bhikkhus that are not shared with bhikkhunīs;
hear them from me exactly as they are.
Six *saṅghādisesa* rules,
eight with the two *aniyata*s,
and twelve *nissaggiya*pācittiya rules.
With those, they become twenty.
There are twenty-two minor rules,
and four offenses entailing confession.
These forty-four [offenses] are not shared by monks with nuns;
there are one hundred and thirty [offenses] for nuns.
Not shared with the bhikkhus;
hear them from me exactly as they are:
the four pārājika offenses.
Ten [offenses] are excluded from the Saṅgha;
twelve are Nissaggiya,
and ninety-six are minor.
There are eight offenses entailing acknowledgment.
Together with these one hundred and thirty,
they are those not shared by bhikkhus among the bhikkhunīs.
One hundred and seventy-six are the qualities not shared by both;
hear them from me exactly as they are.
There are four *pārājika* offenses,
sixteen *saṅghādisesa* offenses,
and two *aniyata* offenses.
There are twenty-four offenses involving forfeiture;
together with one hundred and eighteen,
they are called the minor rules.
The twelve offenses entailing confession:
these one hundred and seventy-six are not shared by both [orders].
Seven hundred and four;
both have the same training—
listen to them as they truly are.
There are four offenses involving defeat (pārājika),
seven offenses requiring formal meeting of the Sangha (saṅghādisesa),
and eighteen offenses entailing forfeiture (nissaggiya).
There are seventy samathas and seventy minor rules (khuddaka);
there are seventy-five rules of training (sekhiya).
These together amount to one hundred and seventy-four.
Both have the same training:
there are eight offenses entailing defeat, which are difficult to approach and comparable to the stump of a palmyra tree.
Like a withered leaf, like a broad stone,
like a man whose head has been cut off,
or like a palm tree severed at its crown.
They do not grow.
There are twenty-three *saṅghādisesa* offenses and two *aniyata* offenses.
There are forty-two offenses entailing relinquishment,
one hundred and eighty-eight offenses of expiation,
and twelve offenses to be confessed.
The seventy-five rules of training are settled by means of the three methods of settling:
through presence and through admission.
And by the method of covering over as with grass.
There are two Uposatha days and two Pavāraṇās;
four formal acts were taught by the Conqueror.
There are exactly five recitations and four [sections];
likewise, there are seven classes of offenses.
There are four legal issues.
They are pacified by seven means of pacification:
by two, four, and three;
the task is accomplished by one.
5. Offenses such as Pārājika:
Listen to what is called "Pārājika" exactly as it is.
Fallen away and defeated,
he is indeed cast out from the true Dhamma;
there is no fellowship with him there.
Therefore this is said:
"Listen to what was called 'an offense entailing suspension' (saṅghādisesa) exactly as it is."
The Saṅgha alone grants probation,
sends back to the beginning,
grants the trial period, and rehabilitates.
Therefore, this is said:
"Listen to what is called 'the undetermined' exactly as it is."
The undetermined is not fixed;
it is a state of non-exclusive possibility;
it is one of three positions.
“He is called ‘undetermined’”;
now listen to what is truly said regarding that which is termed a “grave offense.”
There is no transgression equal to that which one confesses in the presence of another and which the other accepts.
Therefore, this is said:
"Listen to what is called 'an offense entailing relinquishment' exactly as it is."
In the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group,
or alone with another;
having made the formal renunciation, he confesses.
Therefore, this is said:
"Listen to what is called a *pācittiya* exactly as it is."
It casts down wholesome states and transgresses the Noble Path;
it is a point for the delusion of the mind.
Listen to this as it truly is, concerning that which was called "an offense to be confessed" (pāṭidesanīya).
A bhikkhu who is a stranger,
having obtained food with difficulty,
might take it himself and eat it.
It is called "blameworthy.
When eating at invitations,
if one there directs a bhikkhunī according to one's own will, [it is blameworthy].
If one eats there without being invited,
it is called "blameworthy.
Having gone to a family with a mind of faith...
If one who is not ill eats there at a small meal given without invitation,
it is called "blameworthy."
If one dwelling in the forest,
in a place full of suspicion and danger,
should eat there what has not been properly prepared, [he is at fault].
It is called "blameworthy.
When a bhikkhunī who is unrelated [to the owner] takes what belongs to others and is cherished by them;
If a bhikkhunī should herself request ghee, oil, honey, molasses, fish, meat, milk, or curd, [she commits an offense].
They have fallen into censure within the teaching of the Sugata.
Listen now to what is truly meant by that which is called "dukkaṭa" (wrong-doing).
Whatever has been transgressed, missed, stumbled over,
or ill-done— whatever evil a person commits.
Whether in public or in private,
they declare it to be a *dukkaṭa*;
therefore this is so called.
“‘Ill-spoken’— listen to what that truly is:
ill-spoken speech is poorly delivered.”
Whatever state is defiled,
and whatever the wise censure—
by this it is so called.
“Regarding what was said as ‘the trainings’ (sekhiya),
listen to that exactly as it is:
for one who is a learner and is training.”
Following the straight path.
This is the beginning and the conduct;
the mouth is restraint and self-control.
There is no training such as this;
therefore it is said:
"The rain pours down upon the covered."
What is open does not rain upon;
therefore, uncover what is covered,
so that it may not rain upon you.
The forest is the resort of deer,
the sky is the resort of birds,
and non-existence is the resort of all phenomena.
"Nirvana is the destination of the Arahant.
The Collection of Verses is finished.
Its summary:
The fourfold failure prescribed for both monks and nuns in the seven cities;
Common and uncommon;
this is the collection of verses for the sake of favoring the Dispensation.
The Collection of Verses is completed.
